books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic, A. Slavery and the Southern “Way of Life”

primary_sources: John C. Calhoun, "Slavery a Positive Good," Senate speech, February 6, 1837

stimulus.text:
John C. Calhoun, senator from South Carolina, speaking in the Senate on February 6, 1837, during debate over abolitionist petitions:

“But let me not be understood as admitting, even by implication, that the existing relations between the two races in the slaveholding States is an evil:—far otherwise; I hold it to be a good, as it has thus far proved itself to be to both, and will continue to prove so if not disturbed by the fell spirit of abolition.”

“I fearlessly assert that the existing relation between the two races in the South, against which these blind fanatics are waging war, forms the most solid and durable foundation on which to rear free and stable political institutions.”
stimulus.source_note: Quotations verbatim from John C. Calhoun, Senate speech, February 6, 1837, as printed on Wikisource (Slavery a Positive Good). Viewed and checked before writing.

source: original; stimulus verbatim from John C. Calhoun, Senate speech, February 6, 1837, public domain
stem: In the first passage, Calhoun claims that slavery has been a good for whom?

options.text: For slaveholders alone, since only they gained wealth from it
options.misconception: Calhoun does not limit the good to owners; he says it proved good to both races.

options.text: For both enslaved Black people and white slaveholders
For Northern factory owners, who bought cheap Southern cotton
options.misconception: The passage says nothing about Northern factory owners; Calhoun speaks of the two races in the slaveholding states.

options.text: For the federal government, which collected tariffs on cotton exports
options.misconception: The passage says nothing about tariffs or the federal government; Calhoun speaks of the two races, not the treasury.

rationales.A: Calhoun does not limit the good to owners. He says slavery proved itself a good “to both” races.
rationales.B: Calhoun says slavery proved itself a good “to both,” meaning the two races he names, Black and white. He claims enslaved people were improved by it.
rationales.C: The passage says nothing about Northern factory owners. Calhoun speaks of the two races in the slaveholding states.
rationales.D: The passage says nothing about tariffs or the federal government. Calhoun speaks of the two races, not the treasury.
rationales.general:
1. Find the phrase. Calhoun says slavery proved itself a good “to both.”
2. Ask who “both” means. The passage names “the two races in the slaveholding States.”
3. Name the claim. Calhoun argues slavery helped enslaved people as well as owners, so he can call it good rather than a necessary evil.
Background: Calhoun spoke as abolitionist petitions reached the Senate, and he answered them by defending slavery outright.
Remember: when a writer says “both,” check which two groups the passage itself names.
